summary:
We built SPHEREx Sky Change Explorer, a website that lets anyone see how the infrared sky changes over time using real images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission.
You pick a spot in the sky, type a name, or click one of six example targets. Our Python backend finds every SPHEREx image of that spot in NASA’s IRSA archive, lines the images up, removes the background glow and groups them by date. The website then plays them one after another like a flipbook. Stars that stay still look the same, while anything that moved or changed brightness flickers. A difference view shows only what changed, known Gaia stars are circled, and you can click a moving dot to save its position and share a link.
The idea is based on WiseView, which people used to find hundreds of objects in older WISE data. SPHEREx images more than a billion objects, far too many to check by hand. Our tool lets students and amateur astronomers help look through this new data.
details:
What it does: SPHEREx Sky Change Explorer is a website that shows SPHEREx images of the same part of the sky from different dates, one after another. Things that stay still look the same. Anything that moved or changed brightness flickers.

How it works: You pick a target, type coordinates, or enter a name like “M101”. Our Python backend gets all SPHEREx images of that spot from NASA’s IRSA archive. It groups them by date, removes the zodiacal light, and lines them up north-up on one grid so they can be compared. There’s also a difference view that shows only what changed, plus Gaia star labels, motion tracking, and an “I found something moving!” button that saves a shareable link.

Benefits and impact: SPHEREx images over a billion objects, far too many for scientists to check alone. You don’t need to install anything or know how to code to use our tool, so students and amateur astronomers can help find brown dwarfs, fast-moving stars and variable stars.

Tools: Python (FastAPI, astroquery, astropy, NumPy, Pillow), HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Canva, GitHub. Data comes from NASA SPHEREx (IRSA) and ESA Gaia DR3.

Creativity: We took the blink idea from WiseView and adapted it to SPHEREx, which is rotated differently on each visit. Our examples show moving stars, stars that change brightness, and a galaxy that shouldn’t change, which we use to test the tool.

What we considered: We made it fast by caching results, and it automatically retries when NASA’s server is busy. Every image uses the same brightness scale so they can be compared fairly, and the star positions are updated to 2026.
